findings.issue_text: [BUG] The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import time, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` gets the server-start timestamp, not the actual creation time. All cycle-prevention diagnostics and any future staleness logic keyed on `queued` record the wrong time; the value is silently wrong for the entire process lifetime and is nondeterministic across workers/deploys.

[BUG] The task now unconditionally passes `assignment_source=<kwarg>` to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(...)`, but the existing provider implementations (Jira, GitHub, GitLab, VSTS, etc., none modified in this diff) define `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=...)` without an `assignment_source` parameter, raising TypeError on every assignee sync. Every outbound assignee sync task for every provider not updated in this diff crashes with TypeError before the analytics.record call, breaking assignee sync in production even when no assignment_source is present (None is still passed as a keyword).

[BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` puts a raw `datetime` (`queued`) into Celery task kwargs, which the default JSON task serializer cannot encode. When a non-None assignment_source flows through `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, `apply_async` raises `EncodeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable` (with the default json serializer), so the outbound sync task is never enqueued and cross-system assignee propagation silently stops for integration-sourced assignments.

[BUG] `from_dict` catches only (ValueError, TypeError), but a dict whose `queued` value arrives as a JSON string (or any object) still constructs successfully because the dataclass performs no type validation, so corrupt/deserialized payloads pass through silently rather than being rejected. A payload that was serialized to JSON and deserialized elsewhere yields `AssignmentSource(queued='2024-...')` with a string instead of a datetime; any consumer doing datetime arithmetic on `queued` (e.g., staleness checks) crashes downstream, and the test suite's round-trip never exercises this path.

[ADVISORY] The module is placed under `sentry/integrations/services/` but defines no service/handler, and importing it from `sentry/models/groupassignee.py` creates an import from a Django model module into the integrations layer at module load time. Anyone expecting the `services/` package convention (or silo-boundary rules about models importing integration code) is bitten when refactoring; the model-layer import also makes `groupassignee` fail at import if this module ever grows region-silo dependencies.

[ADVISORY] The test `test_from_dict_inalid_data` (typo 'inalid') and `test_from_dict_empty_array` both exercise only failure paths of `from_dict`; no test covers round-tripping through the Celery kwargs path where `queued` becomes a non-datetime, which is the path the production code actually uses. The coverage gap hides the serialization defect in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` — a regression in the JSON round-trip would break integration-sourced assignee sync in production with no failing test.

[BUG] The `queued` field default is `timezone.now()` evaluated once at class-definition (import) time, so every AssignmentSource instance records the process import time, not the actual queue time. Any future use of `queued` for staleness/debugging measures against a timestamp frozen at worker boot; all instances share one value.

[BUG] `to_dict()` uses `asdict()`, which leaves `queued` as a raw `datetime` object inside the Celery `apply_async` kwargs in sync.py, and a JSON-serialized Celery transport cannot serialize datetime. sync_group_assignee_outbound.apply_async raises a EncodeError (or silently mis-serializes) on JSON-serialized queues, breaking outbound assignee sync entirely for any assignment carrying an assignment_source.

[BUG] After a JSON round-trip through the queue, `queued` arrives as an ISO string, so `cls(**input_dict)` raises `TypeError` (datetime constructor rejects a string) which `from_dict` swallows and returns None, silently disabling cycle prevention. The diff's core feature — sync-cycle prevention — is turned off for every queued task that actually traverses a serializer: an inbound assignment from Jira propagates back to Jira, re-triggering inbound sync, creating the assignment ping-pong loop the diff claims to prevent.

[ADVISORY] `from_dict` returns None on any malformed payload with no logging, so corrupt/legacy task payloads silently degrade to 'no source' behavior. Operators debugging sync loops get no signal that the cycle-prevention payload failed to parse; the fallback is exactly the looping behavior the feature exists to stop.

[ADVISORY] `sync_status_outbound` was given an `assignment_source` parameter, but no caller in the diff (or the status-sync path in sync_status_inbound/GroupHistory) ever constructs or passes one, and no test covers status-cycle prevention. Status resolve/unresolve loops between Sentry and the external tracker remain un-prevented while the PR's stated goal is cross-system sync-cycle prevention; the parameter is a ships-inert hook with no producer.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a test only for the matching-integration suppression case; there is no test that an assignment originating from a *different* integration still propagates outward, despite the code comment in should_sync explicitly promising 'This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward'. A regression that over-suppresses cross-integration propagation (e.g., comparing provider name instead of integration_id) would pass the entire new test suite; multi-integration customers silently lose assignee sync.

[ADVISORY] The base `IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` silently accepts and ignores the new `sync_source` argument and always returns False, while other should_sync overrides not in this diff (e.g., per-provider overrides) still have the single-argument signature and will never receive source-aware cycle checks. Cycle prevention applies only to the generic IssueSyncIntegration path; any provider overriding should_sync keeps the old behavior, giving inconsistent loop prevention across integrations on the same assignment path.

[BUG] `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates the default at module import time, so every `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` gets the process-start timestamp, not queue time. The `queued` timestamp is meaningless (it reflects when the worker/process imported the module), so any consumer relying on it for staleness or ordering decisions gets wrong data; also the mutable-default-style trap misleads future readers adding non-immutable defaults.

[BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` produces `{'queued': <datetime>, ...}` which is passed through `apply_async` kwargs (sync.py:137-141), but `AssignmentSource.from_dict` reconstructs via `cls(**input_dict)`, which raises TypeError on a string/float `queued` and returns None, silently discarding the source. When the task broker serializes kwargs to JSON (or any non-pickle transport), either the enqueue fails outright, or after deserialization `from_dict` returns None and `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)` returns True — the cycle-pretection the diff exists to provide is silently disabled on exactly the cross-process path it was built for.

[ADVISORY] The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter that no caller in this diff passes and no docstring explains, expanding the status-sync surface with inert, untraceable work. Every out-of-tree subclass of `IssueSyncIntegration` must now accept a kwarg whose purpose is undefined for status sync; all in-tree call sites still invoke it without `assignment_source`, so the parameter is dead code that a future refactor will either have to wire through or delete, and reviewers cannot trace it to the assignee-sync requirement stated in the PR.

[ADVISORY] Only the assign path of `sync_group_assignee_inbound` threads `assignment_source` through to `GroupAssignee.objects.assign`, but the deassign path (line 96) and every other inbound caller of `assign`/`deassign` (e.g. auto-assignment, API endpoints) pass `assignment_source=None`, so cycle detection only covers inbound assign. An inbound unassign from integration X still triggers `sync_group_assignee_outbound(group, None, assign=False, assignment_source=None)`, which calls `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)` → True and unassigns the very same external issue in X, re-firing X's inbound webhook — the sync loop the diff claims to prevent is only half-closed, and operators with bidirectional assignee sync on two integrations still get ping-pong on unassign.

[ADVISORY] The serialization round-trip that the Celery path depends on (dict → JSON-safe transport → `from_dict`) is untested; `test_to_dict` only asserts the datetime key exists and never feeds the result back through `from_dict`. A regression that breaks `queued` datetime serialization (already latent per the finding above) ships undetected, because no test in the diff exercises `to_dict` output through `from_dict` — the exact transformation performed in `sync_assignee_outbound`'s task body.

[BUG] The `queued` field default `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition (import) time, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` — including all instances built via `from_integration` — carries the process's import timestamp, not the time the assignment was made. Any future consumer relying on `queued` to measure sync latency or detect stale sync loops gets a garbage, monotonically-frozen timestamp; the existing test `test_to_dict` asserting `queued is not None` passes anyway, so the defect ships green.

[BUG] The task calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)` with a new keyword argument, but this diff updates no concrete implementer of `sync_assignee_outbound` (Jira, GitHub, GitLab, VSTS, etc.) to accept it — the diff only changed the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature — so every provider implementation whose signature lacks `assignment_source` or `**kwargs` raises TypeError at runtime. Outbound assignee sync for any provider without a compatible signature crashes in the Celery worker, so assignee changes silently stop propagating to linked external issues for that provider.

[ADVISORY] Format-drift between writer and reader: `to_dict()`/`asdict()` emits `queued` as a `datetime` object, but the dict crosses a Celery task boundary in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`; under a JSON task serializer (or any JSON logging/enqueue step) the datetime fails to serialize or arrives as a string, and `from_dict` performs no type validation so `queued` becomes a `str` silently. With a JSON-based Celery serializer the task dispatch raises a serialization error for every sourced assignment; with string round-trips, any consumer of `queued` comparing or formatting it gets inconsistent types depending on transport path.

[ADVISORY] The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gained `assignment_source`, but this diff never passes `assignment_source` to any `sync_status_outbound` call site nor wires `sync_status_inbound` to produce one, so the status-sync cycle-prevention half of the design is inert: the new parameter is an unused dead knob on the status path while only assignee sync is protected. Status change loops between two integrations (A resolves → B inbound → B outbound → A) remain unguarded; the design implies cross-system cycle prevention was implemented but only one of the two sync dimensions actually carries the source.

[ADVISORY] `from_dict` only catches `(ValueError, TypeError)` and does not validate types, so a payload where `integration_id` is a string (e.g. `"123"` after JSON round-trip through a generic serialization layer) constructs an `AssignmentSource` with a string `integration_id`, which then fails the `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` int comparison in `should_sync` and the cycle guard silently never trips. A malformed or lossy payload silently disables the echo-prevention guard instead of surfacing the corruption, reintroducing the sync loop the feature exists to stop.

[BUG] The `queued` field default is `timezone.now()` evaluated once at class-definition (import) time, and `to_dict()` serializes it as a raw datetime into Celery task kwargs. Two failures: (1) every AssignmentSource instance forever reports the process-import timestamp rather than queue time, so the field is meaningless; (2) `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (sync.py) calls `assignment_source.to_dict()` into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`, and with the default JSON task serializer a `datetime` in kwargs raises EncodeError, so every source-tagged outbound assignee sync fails to enqueue and assignee propagation silently stops for all inbound-originated assignments.

[BUG] `from_dict` swallows deserialization failures by returning None, which `sync_assignee_outbound` (tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py:53-55) then passes to `should_sync` as `sync_source=None`, disabling the cycle-prevention check entirely. Any malformed or partially-drifted payload (e.g. a key renamed in a later version, or a dict produced by a non-JSON round-trip of the datetime `queued` field) causes the source tag to vanish and the inbound-triggered assignment to be synced back out to the very integration that originated it — the exact infinite sync loop this change exists to prevent, reintroduced silently with no log or error.

[ADVISORY] `from_dict` does no type validation, so a payload with `integration_id` as a string (e.g. after a JSON round-trip through some transports) constructs an AssignmentSource whose `integration_id` never equals the integer `self.org_integration.integration_id`, defeating the equality check in `should_sync` (issues.py:389-390). Operators debugging 'why is my sync looping' get no signal: the dataclass constructs happily, the comparison silently fails, and cycle prevention is off — the failure mode is indistinguishable from the feature not existing. A strict `from_dict` (or type coercion) is needed for the guard to be trustworthy.

[BUG] Cycle prevention is only wired through the assignee path: `sync_status_outbound` gained an `assignment_source` parameter in its abstract signature, but no caller in this diff ever passes one, `should_sync` for status attributes is never called with a `sync_source`, and the inbound status path (sync_status_inbound) never records an AssignmentSource — so the diff's stated objective ("prevent sync-cycles") is enforced for assignee sync only. A status change arriving inbound from integration A still triggers `sync_status_outbound` back to integration A (and to any linked integration, which then syncs back), reproducing the same ping-pong loop the change claims to close, just on the status axis instead of assignee. The added abstract parameter also silently changes the contract for every out-of-tree subclass implementation without any implementation or caller being updated in this diff.

[BUG] AssignmentSource.to_dict() emits a raw datetime for the 'queued' field, which is placed into Celery task kwargs via apply_async in sync.py, breaking on any JSON-based serializer and silently degrading on round-trip. In sync.py the dict built by to_dict() (containing a datetime object) is passed as assignment_source_dict in apply_async kwargs; with a JSON serializer the task enqueue raises EncodeError and the assignee sync never runs; even with pickle, from_dict on the deserialized payload only works because asdict keeps the datetime — but if the payload is ever logged, serialized to JSON elsewhere, or persisted, the datetime becomes a string and from_dict returns a None-equivalent mismatch, dropping the cycle-prevention source and re-enabling the integration-to-itself sync loop this diff was written to prevent.

[ADVISORY] The 'queued' field uses timezone.now() as a dataclass default, evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit queued value shares the import-time timestamp. Any future use of 'queued' for staleness/replay decisions (the field's evident purpose) will compute against a stale import-time clock; operators debugging sync cycles get misleading queue times. The default should be a field(default_factory=timezone.now).

[ADVISORY] from_dict performs cls(**input_dict) on an unvalidated dict from task kwargs with no type or field validation beyond TypeError/ValueError, and treats any malformed payload as None (no logging). A payload with extra keys, string integration_id, or a string 'queued' (post-JSON round-trip) either silently returns None — which disables the sync-cycle guard, resurrecting the infinite integration-to-itself assign loop the diff exists to fix — or constructs a source with a non-int integration_id that never matches, same effect. There is no signal (log/metric) when the guard silently degrades, so a serialization drift turns into a hard-to-diagnose sync storm.

[BUG] The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates the default once at class-definition (module import) time, so every AssignmentSource ever constructed carries the server's import timestamp, not the time the assignment was queued. Any consumer relying on `queued` gets a stale, identical timestamp for the whole process lifetime; the new test `test_to_dict` (tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:32) asserts only `result.get("queued") is not None` — an existence-only assertion that passes even though the value is wrong, so the suite provides false confidence for the one field whose semantics are broken.

[BUG] `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` — which contains a raw `datetime` in the `queued` key — directly into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`, which the default JSON task serializer cannot serialize. Every assignment that originates from an integration sync raises `TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable` at enqueue time, silently dropping the outbound sync. Both new tests mock `ExampleIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` (tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:154, 160) and the in-test `self.tasks()` runner executes inline without enforcing JSON serialization, so the tests never exercise the celery serialization path that the diff's real production behavior depends on.

[ADVISORY] The `should_sync` branch where `sync_source` is present but has a *different* `integration_id` (the 'still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward' path the comment promises) has no test that exercises it. I checked tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py and tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py — the only new cross-integration test (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration`) covers only the matching-id rejection; if the equality check were inverted or over-broadened (e.g. `if sync_source:` returning False unconditionally), all new tests would still pass, shipping a regression that silently stops outbound assignee sync for all other integrations.

[ADVISORY] The `assignment_source` parameter added to `deassign` and threaded into `sync_group_assignee_outbound(group, None, assign=False, ...)` is never tested with a non-None value — the deassign test (tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:271-274) only asserts `assignment_source=None` is passed through. The unassign half of the cycle-prevention feature is unverified: `sync_group_assignee_inbound`'s `deassign` path (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:96-100) constructs an AssignmentSource, but no test confirms that an inbound unassign does not echo back out as an outbound unassign; a bug there (e.g. `deassign` dropping the kwarg) reopens the sync loop for unassignments while the suite stays green. Checked tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py and tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py — neither covers this path.

[BUG] sync_group_assignee_outbound passes assignment_source.to_dict(), which contains a raw datetime in the `queued` field, as Celery task kwargs, and the default JSON task serializer cannot encode datetime. AssignmentSource.to_dict() (assignment_source.py:23-29) uses asdict(), leaving `queued` as a datetime object. When any integration-driven assignment flows through sync_group_assignee_outbound (i.e., every inbound assignee sync once this diff ships), apply_async raises EncodeError (kombu CannotEncodeJson / Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable), so the sync_assignee_outbound task is never enqueued and the assignee change is never propagated outward — the cross-system sync this PR exists to implement silently no-ops for the sourced path.

[ADVISORY] The `queued` field's default is `timezone.now()` evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource created in a process shares the same process-start timestamp. Dataclass defaults are evaluated at class-definition time, not per-instantiation: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs when assignment_source.py is first imported. All sources built via from_integration carry the worker process's boot time rather than the actual assignment time, so any future use of `queued` for staleness/cycle detection (its only plausible purpose) computes wrong ages — e.g., a long-lived region-silo worker stamps every inbound sync with hours-old timestamps. The author's likely counter is that `queued` is currently unused downstream; but shipping a field whose value is wrong by construction guarantees misinterpretation the moment someone reads it. Fix is mechanical: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

[ADVISORY] from_dict returns None for any malformed payload, silently discarding the assignment source instead of surfacing the corruption. If a task queue message carries a payload where `queued` deserializes to a string (JSON round-trip of the datetime, once the serialization bug above is fixed) or any drifted schema, from_dict swallows it via `cls(**input_dict)` failing with TypeError and returns None — should_sync then treats the sync as unsourced and re-propagates to the originating integration, re-creating the sync cycle this PR was written to prevent. The cycle-suppression guarantee degrades to a no-op under exactly the payload drift that silent retries/version skew produce. The counter-argument is fail-open is deliberate for robustness; but fail-open on the anti-loop guard means the failure mode is the loop, so a logged warning or strict parse is warranted.

As shown in the diff, there is no runtime type validation/coercion for `queued`, so a payload like `{"source_name": "x", "integration_id": 1, "queued": "2024-..."}` would construct successfully with `queued` as a `str`. A payload with extra keys, string integration_id, or a string 'queued' (post-JSON round-trip) either silently returns None — which disables the sync-cycle guard, resurrecting the infinite integration-to-itself assign loop the diff exists to fix — or constructs a source with a non-int integration_id that never matches, same effect. There is no signal (log/metric) when the guard silently degrades, so a serialization drift turns into a hard-to-diagnose sync storm.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AssignmentSource.from_dict` doing `cls(**input_dict)` with only `TypeError/ValueError` handling and no explicit field/type validation or logging. Because dataclass type hints aren’t enforced at runtime, a payload like `{"integration_id": "123", "source_name": "x"}` would successfully construct an `AssignmentSource` with a string `integration_id`, and `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source)` would then fail the equality check against the int `self.org_integration.integration_id`, effectively bypassing the cycle guard. However, the diff’s in-tree producer (`to_dict()` from `from_integration()`) supplies an int `integration_id`, so an actual regression/infinite loop from the shown code path isn’t directly verifiable from the diff alone; it’s a robustness/diagnostics gap around malformed/changed serialization.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates the default once at class-definition (module import) time, so every AssignmentSource ever constructed carries the server's import timestamp, not the time the assignment was queued. Any consumer relying on `queued` gets a stale, identical timestamp for the whole process lifetime; the new test `test_to_dict` (tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:32) asserts only `result.get("queued") is not None` — an existence-only assertion that passes even though the value is wrong, so the suite provides false confidence for the one field whose semantics are broken.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`, the dataclass defines `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`, which calls `timezone.now()` at class definition/import time, making `queued` a single shared timestamp for all `AssignmentSource` instances created in that process. This is a real correctness defect; the intended behavior is almost certainly per-instance creation time (would require `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`). The added test `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued` is present, so it would not catch this broken semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` — which contains a raw `datetime` in the `queued` key — directly into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`, which the default JSON task serializer cannot serialize. Every assignment that originates from an integration sync raises `TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable` at enqueue time, silently dropping the outbound sync. Both new tests mock `ExampleIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` (tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:154, 160) and the in-test `self.tasks()` runner executes inline without enforcing JSON serialization, so the tests never exercise the celery serialization path that the diff's real production behavior depends on.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` return `asdict(self)`, which includes the `queued` field. `queued` is a `datetime` (declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` in `AssignmentSource`), and `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` directly into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`. If the task serializer is JSON (a common/default Celery config), a raw `datetime` in `kwargs` will not be JSON-serializable and would fail at enqueue/serialization time. The added tests run tasks inline (`with self.tasks():`) and thus would not necessarily exercise Celery's serialization path, so they wouldn't catch this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `should_sync` branch where `sync_source` is present but has a *different* `integration_id` (the 'still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward' path the comment promises) has no test that exercises it. I checked tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py and tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py — the only new cross-integration test (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration`) covers only the matching-id rejection; if the equality check were inverted or over-broadened (e.g. `if sync_source:` returning False unconditionally), all new tests would still pass, shipping a regression that silently stops outbound assignee sync for all other integrations.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new nontrivial control flow in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(...)` that short-circuits only when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`, with an explicit comment that other integrations should still propagate changes outward. The updated tests in `tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py` cover (a) `assignment_source=None` (expects outbound sync called with `assignment_source=None`) and (b) matching integration-id rejection (`assert_not_called()`), but there is no test that passes a non-None `AssignmentSource` whose `integration_id` differs from the target integration to ensure outbound sync still occurs. That’s a concrete, diff-grounded test gap for newly added logic, not a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `assignment_source` parameter added to `deassign` and threaded into `sync_group_assignee_outbound(group, None, assign=False, ...)` is never tested with a non-None value — the deassign test (tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:271-274) only asserts `assignment_source=None` is passed through. The unassign half of the cycle-prevention feature is unverified: `sync_group_assignee_inbound`'s `deassign` path (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:96-100) constructs an AssignmentSource, but no test confirms that an inbound unassign does not echo back out as an outbound unassign; a bug there (e.g. `deassign` dropping the kwarg) reopens the sync loop for unassignments while the suite stays green. Checked tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py and tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py — neither covers this path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `assignment_source` plumbing for both assign/deassign and uses it for loop prevention in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source)` (returns False if `sync_source.integration_id` matches the org integration). Tests added cover the non-None `assignment_source` case only for **assign** (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` asserts no outbound sync). The existing **deassign** test still asserts `assignment_source=None` is passed (`assert_called_with(..., assign=False, assignment_source=None)`), and there is no test exercising `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(..., assignment_source=...)` (as used by `sync_group_assignee_inbound`’s unassign branch) to ensure it prevents an outbound unassign sync. So the finding about an unverified unassign/cycle-prevention path is accurate and diff-grounded, but it’s a missing-test coverage issue rather than a demonstrated defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] sync_group_assignee_outbound passes assignment_source.to_dict(), which contains a raw datetime in the `queued` field, as Celery task kwargs, and the default JSON task serializer cannot encode datetime. AssignmentSource.to_dict() (assignment_source.py:23-29) uses asdict(), leaving `queued` as a datetime object. When any integration-driven assignment flows through sync_group_assignee_outbound (i.e., every inbound assignee sync once this diff ships), apply_async raises EncodeError (kombu CannotEncodeJson / Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable), so the sync_assignee_outbound task is never enqueued and the assignee change is never propagated outward — the cross-system sync this PR exists to implement silently no-ops for the sourced path.

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)` (new file `assignment_source.py`), which includes the `queued: datetime` field as a raw `datetime` object. `sync_group_assignee_outbound()` then passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` directly into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)` as `assignment_source_dict` (`integrations/utils/sync.py`). If the Celery task serializer is JSON (common default), a raw `datetime` in kwargs is not JSON-serializable, so enqueuing the task would fail. The diff itself clearly shows the non-serialized datetime flowing into Celery kwargs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `queued` field's default is `timezone.now()` evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource created in a process shares the same process-start timestamp. Dataclass defaults are evaluated at class-definition time, not per-instantiation: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs when assignment_source.py is first imported. All sources built via from_integration carry the worker process's boot time rather than the actual assignment time, so any future use of `queued` for staleness/cycle detection (its only plausible purpose) computes wrong ages — e.g., a long-lived region-silo worker stamps every inbound sync with hours-old timestamps. The author's likely counter is that `queued` is currently unused downstream; but shipping a field whose value is wrong by construction guarantees misinterpretation the moment someone reads it. Fix is mechanical: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` the dataclass field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. This calls `timezone.now()` at class definition/import time, so every `AssignmentSource` instance created without explicitly passing `queued` (including via `from_integration`) will share the same timestamp for the lifetime of that Python process. The correct per-instance behavior requires `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] from_dict returns None for any malformed payload, silently discarding the assignment source instead of surfacing the corruption. If a task queue message carries a payload where `queued` deserializes to a string (JSON round-trip of the datetime, once the serialization bug above is fixed) or any drifted schema, from_dict swallows it via `cls(**input_dict)` failing with TypeError and returns None — should_sync then treats the sync as unsourced and re-propagates to the originating integration, re-creating the sync cycle this PR was written to prevent. The cycle-suppression guarantee degrades to a no-op under exactly the payload drift that silent retries/version skew produce. The counter-argument is fail-open is deliberate for robustness; but fail-open on the anti-loop guard means the failure mode is the loop, so a logged warning or strict parse is warranted.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AssignmentSource.from_dict` intentionally returns `None` on `ValueError`/`TypeError` (silent fail-open), and `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source)` only suppresses cycles when a non-`None` `sync_source` is provided. So if the payload is missing/has wrong keys (e.g. no `integration_id`), parsing will yield `None` and the anti-loop guard is bypassed. However, the finding’s concrete example that a JSON-stringified `queued` datetime would cause `TypeError` and thus return `None` is not supported by the diff: dataclasses don’t enforce type hints at runtime, so `queued` being a string would still construct successfully and preserve `integration_id` for the guard. This makes the concern more of a robustness/observability design issue (log/strict parse) than a directly verifiable defect from the shown changes.
